rejected.title: Functions of the skeleton
card: Support and protection
The skeleton gives the body its shape and holds up the soft tissues. It also protects organs, such as the skull around the brain and the ribs around the heart and lungs.
Movement
Bones act as levers. When a muscle pulls on a bone, the bone moves around a joint.
Storage
Bones store minerals, mainly calcium and phosphorus. The body releases them into the blood when it needs them.
Blood cell production
Red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are made in the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside some bones.
rejected.remember: The skeleton holds, guards and moves the body, and it stores minerals and makes blood cells.

a.q: Which function of the skeleton is shown by the ribs surrounding the lungs?
a.why: The ribs form a cage around the heart and lungs, which shields these organs from knocks. Support is the most tempting answer, because bones do hold the body up. But here the ribs are guarding soft organs, which is protection.
a.clue: Focus on the lungs, not the shape of the whole body.

b.q: For a few weeks, Ella eats very little calcium. Tests show the calcium level in her blood stays normal. Which skeleton function explains this?
opts: Bones store calcium and release it into the blood
Bone marrow makes new cells and adds them to the blood
Bones act as levers that pump blood around the body
Bones support the soft tissues that carry the blood
b.why: Bones store minerals such as calcium and release them into the blood when the body needs them, so the level can stay steady when little comes from food. Making blood cells is tempting because it also involves the blood, but it produces cells, not minerals like calcium.
b.clue: Think about where the calcium in her blood came from.

b.q: Jay breaks his thigh bone. A doctor says his body may be short of new red blood cells for a while. Which skeleton function is linked to this?
opts: Bones act as levers for movement
Bones store calcium for the blood
Bones protect the organs inside them
b.why: Red blood cells are made in bone marrow, which is inside some bones, so damage to a bone can affect that function. Storing calcium is tempting because it also involves the blood, but calcium is a mineral and not a blood cell.
b.clue: Which function produces cells, not just stores something?

problems.detail: The scenario is medically misleading. A broken thigh bone does not normally leave a person short of new red blood cells because the marrow stops working. Any shortfall after a femur fracture comes mainly from blood loss. In adults, the femur shaft holds mostly yellow marrow, and red cells are made across many bones. Students may learn a false cause-and-effect link.
The clue 'Which function produces cells, not just stores something?' points straight to the only option about making cells, so it gives the answer away.
The clue 'Think about what the ribs keep safe' all but names protection, so a student can answer without knowing the idea.
The distractor 'Bones protect the organs inside them' is confusing, because bones protect organs around or beneath them, not organs inside the bones.

check.summary: The card and question a are accurate, but both clues give the answers away. Question b's scenario wrongly suggests a broken thigh bone causes a shortage of new red blood cells through lost marrow production; it should be rewritten with a sound example.
